title: The Mummy That Waited 3,000 Years
blurb: Salt, linen, and seventy days of work. How ancient Egypt made a body last, and why the curse is the only make-believe part.

blocks.prompt: How to Make a Mummy
blocks.text: A mummy starts as a real body. Long ago in Egypt, people wanted the body to last forever. First they took out the wet parts inside. Then they covered the body in salt. The salt is called natron. It pulled all the water out. After forty days the body was dry. Then came the wrapping. People wound long strips of linen around and around, layer after layer. It took many days. At the end they put a mask over the face so everyone would know who it was. Then the mummy went into its tomb to rest.

blocks.prompt: Seventy Days to Make a Mummy
blocks.text: Making a mummy took seventy days, and every one of them had a job. The body was carried to a tent by the river. Priests took out the lungs, the liver, the stomach, and the guts, because wet parts rot first. Each one went into its own stone jar. The brain came out through the nose with a long hooked rod, and it was thrown away. The Egyptians thought people did their thinking with the heart, so the heart stayed right where it was. Then the body was packed in natron, a salt that people scooped from dry lake beds. Natron drinks water. For forty days it pulled every drop out of the skin. What was left was light and dry and would not rot. Now the wrapping could start. Strips of linen went around each finger, each toe, then the arms, then the whole body, layer over layer, with lucky charms tucked between them. Sticky resin glued it all together. On day seventy the mummy went into its coffin, and the coffin went into the tomb.

4.title: The Mummy That Waited 3,000 Years
4.subtitle: A reading and history sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Rotting needs water, warmth, and air

Bog bodies keep their skin, hair, and last meal
Egypt's first mummies were made by hot sand
The Chinchorro of Chile got there first

blocks.prompt: The Mummies Nobody Made
blocks.text: Egypt gets the credit, but Egypt did not invent the mummy, and most mummies were never made on purpose. A body rots because bacteria inside it get to work, and bacteria need water, warmth, and air. Take away any one of those and the body simply stops changing. Nature takes them away all the time. On a September day in 1991, two hikers in the Alps found a man lying face down in melting ice. They assumed he was a lost climber. He was 5,300 years old. Ice had held him at a steady cold since the Stone Age, and he still had his clothes, his shoes, his copper axe, and the tattoos on his back. Scientists named him Otzi, after the valley. Peat bogs work a different way. Bog water is cold, acidic, and holds almost no oxygen, so bodies dropped into northern European bogs come out centuries later with eyelashes, stubble, and the last meal still in the stomach. Dry sand works too, and that is where Egypt's story really begins. Long before any priest picked up a knife, Egyptians buried their dead in shallow desert graves. The sand pulled the water out and left the bodies preserved. Later Egyptians started building fancier tombs, the bodies rotted inside them, and the priests had to work out how to copy what plain sand had been doing free of charge. Egypt was not even first at doing it on purpose. Along the desert coast of what is now northern Chile, the Chinchorro people were taking bodies apart, drying them, and rebuilding them with sticks, clay, and ash about two thousand years before the earliest Egyptian tried it.

5.title: The Mummy That Waited 3,000 Years
5.subtitle: A reading and history sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Mummy comes from mumiya, a word for tar

blocks.prompt: The Long Afterlife of Egyptian Mummies
blocks.text: The Egyptians who wrapped a body expected it to lie undisturbed forever. Almost none of them got that. Start with the name. Our word mummy comes from mumiya, a Persian and Arabic word for bitumen, the black tar that seeps out of the ground and was sold as medicine. Some Egyptian mummies were coated in dark resin that had hardened into a similar black crust, and traders decided the two substances must be the same thing. They were not. But by the twelfth century, European apothecaries were grinding up genuine Egyptian dead, bottling the powder, and selling it as a cure for bruises, epilepsy, and stomach pain. Demand ran so far ahead of supply that dealers in Alexandria began faking it with fresh bodies, tar, and a hot oven. Painters found another use. A pigment called mummy brown, made from ground mummy mixed with white pitch and myrrh, sat on artists' palettes in Europe for hundreds of years. It gave a warm transparent shade that painters liked. Many of them had no idea what was in the tube. When the painter Edward Burne-Jones learned the truth, he carried his tube out to the garden and buried it. In Victorian Britain, the fashion turned to entertainment. A gentleman would buy a mummy, invite guests, and unwrap it in his drawing room while a doctor narrated. Each party destroyed, in one evening, a body that had survived three thousand years. Today the tools are gentler and the results are better. A CT scanner can slice a wrapped mummy into thousands of images and rebuild it on a screen without lifting a single bandage. In 2021 researchers digitally unwrapped Pharaoh Amenhotep I, who died around 1500 BC and had not been touched since ancient priests rewrapped him about three thousand years ago. They found his face, his teeth, thirty amulets, and the repairs those priests had made to damage done by tomb robbers. Not one bandage was lifted.

6.title: The Mummy That Waited 3,000 Years
6.subtitle: A reading and history sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Tutankhamun's tomb was opened in November 1922
Lord Carnarvon died of an infected mosquito bite
No curse inscription was ever found at the tomb
Howard Carter lived another sixteen years
A 2002 study found no effect on lifespans
Mummy is from mumiya, a Persian word for tar

blocks.prompt: The Curse That Was Never There
blocks.text: On the morning of November 26, 1922, Howard Carter cut a small hole in a sealed doorway in the Valley of the Kings, pushed a candle through it, and looked into a room no living person had entered for more than three thousand years. His patron, Lord Carnarvon, standing behind him, asked whether he could see anything. Carter's answer became the most quoted line in the history of archaeology: "Yes, wonderful things." The following April, Carnarvon was dead. He had cut a mosquito bite while shaving, the wound became infected, blood poisoning set in, pneumonia followed, and he died in a Cairo hotel at the age of fifty-six. Antibiotics did not yet exist. Thousands of people died of infected wounds every year, and nobody wrote about them. The newspapers wrote about this one. Within days the story was no longer about a man and a mosquito. It was about a curse, an ancient warning, a pharaoh reaching out of the dark to punish the men who had disturbed him. Reporters claimed an inscription over the tomb door promised death to anyone who entered. No such inscription has ever been found. Reporters claimed the lights of Cairo went out at the moment Carnarvon died. The lights of Cairo went out regularly. The novelist Marie Corelli had already warned in print that dire punishment awaited intruders, and Arthur Conan Doyle, who believed in fairies, told journalists that an angry spirit might be responsible. The story was too good to check. It has been checked since. In 2002 an epidemiologist named Mark Nelson identified the twenty-five Westerners who were present when the tomb, the burial chamber, or the coffin was opened, and compared how long they lived against others of the same age and background who were not there. He found no difference worth reporting. Howard Carter, the man who actually opened the burial chamber and lifted the lid on the coffin, lived another sixteen years and died at sixty-four of natural causes. The curse, if it existed, had spectacularly poor aim. There is a smaller, stranger truth underneath the invented one. Sealed tombs can hold mold. Aspergillus spores survive a long time in dry, still air, and a person with a weak immune system who breathes them in can become seriously ill. Carnarvon was not a healthy man. He had spent years recovering from a car crash and had come to Egypt in the first place because the dry air was kind to his damaged lungs. It is possible, though not proven, that the tomb air did him no favors. That is the honest version, and it is worth noticing what happened to it: nobody made a movie about a fungus. The curse story has cost something real. It teaches people that mummies are monsters, when a mummy is a person somebody loved enough to spend seventy days and a fortune preserving. It handed gift shops a bandaged villain and handed museums a problem. And it buried the actual question Carter's candle raised, which no curse can answer: what do we owe the dead when they cannot object to what we do with them?
